title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter 13
paragraphs: When Pierre and his wife came into the drawing room, the countess was in one of her usual moods, the kind that needed the mental effort of a game of patience, and so—though out of sheer habit she greeted him with the words she always used whenever Pierre or her son came back after an absence: "High time, my dear, high time! We were all tired of waiting for you. Well, thank God!" and received her presents with another of her customary remarks: "It's not the gift that matters, my dear, but that you gave it to me, an old woman..."—still, it was plain she was not really pleased at Pierre's arrival just then, since it drew her attention away from the unfinished game.

She finished her game of patience before she even examined the presents. They consisted of a card box of splendid workmanship, a bright-blue Sèvres teacup painted with shepherdesses and fitted with a lid, and a gold snuffbox with the count's portrait on the lid, which Pierre had commissioned from a miniaturist in Petersburg. The countess had long wanted a box of just that kind, but, not wanting to cry just then, she glanced indifferently at the portrait and gave her chief attention to the card box.

"Thank you, my dear, you've cheered me up," she said, as she always did. "But best of all, you've brought yourself back—I never saw anything like it, you really ought to give your wife a scolding! What are we to do with her? She's like a madwoman when you're away. Doesn't see anything, doesn't remember anything," she went on, repeating her usual phrases. "Look, Anna Timofeyevna," she added, turning to her companion, "see what a card box my son has brought us!"
Belova admired the presents and was delighted with her dress material.

Though Pierre, Natasha, Nicholas, Countess Mary, and Denisov had a great deal to talk over that they could not discuss in front of the old countess—not that anything was hidden from her, but because she had fallen so far behind in so many things that if they had started talking in her presence, they would have had to answer questions that made no sense anymore, and repeat things they had already told her many times over: that so-and-so was dead, that so-and-so had married, all of which she would once again be unable to remember—still, out of habit, they all sat down to tea around the samovar in the drawing room, and Pierre answered the countess's questions about whether Prince Vasili had aged, and whether Countess Mary Alexeyevna sent her greetings and still thought of them, and other matters that interested no one, including the countess herself.

This kind of conversation, interesting to no one and yet unavoidable, went on all through teatime. All the grown members of the family had gathered around the round tea table, where Sonya presided over the samovar. The children, with their tutors and governesses, had already had their tea, and their voices could be heard from the next room. At tea, everyone sat in their accustomed places: Nicholas by the stove, at a small table where his tea was brought to him; Milka, the old gray borzoi bitch, daughter of the first Milka, her face now quite gray and her large black eyes seeming more prominent than ever, lay in the armchair beside him; Denisov, his curly hair, mustache, and whiskers now half gray, sat beside Countess Mary, his general's tunic unbuttoned; Pierre sat between his wife and the old countess. He talked about the things he knew would interest the old lady and that she could follow. He told her of goings-on in society, and about the people who had once made up the circle of her contemporaries, a real, living, distinct group, but who were now for the most part scattered about the world, and, like herself, were gathering in the last ears of the harvests they had sown in earlier years. But to the old countess, those contemporaries of hers still seemed the only serious, real society there was. Natasha could tell, from how animated Pierre was, that his visit had been eventful and that he had a great deal to tell them, but did not dare say it in front of the old countess. Denisov, not being a member of the family, did not grasp Pierre's caution, and, being a malcontent deeply interested in what was going on in Petersburg, kept pressing Pierre to tell them what was happening in the Semyonovsky regiment, then about Arakcheev, then about the Bible Society. Once or twice Pierre got carried away and began speaking of these things, but Nicholas and Natasha always steered him back to the health of Prince Ivan and Countess Mary Alexeyevna.
"Well, and all this idiocy—Gossner and Tatáwinova? Is that weally still going on?" Denisov asked.
"Going on?" Pierre exclaimed. "Why, more than ever! The Bible Society is running the whole government now!"

"What's that, mon cher ami?" asked the countess, who had finished her tea and plainly needed a pretext for being angry now that her meal was done. "What's this about the government? I don't understand."

"Well, you know, Maman," Nicholas put in, knowing just how to translate things into his mother's language, "Prince Alexander Golitsyn has founded a society, and as a result he has great influence, they say."
"Arakcheev and Golitsyn," Pierre put in, without thinking, "are the whole government now! And what a government! They see treason everywhere and are afraid of everything."

"Well, and how is Prince Alexander to blame? He's a most estimable man. I used to meet him at Mary Antonovna's," the countess said, in an offended tone; and, still more offended that everyone had fallen silent, she went on: "These days everyone finds fault with everything. A Gospel Society! Well, and what's the harm in that?" and she rose—everyone else got up too—and, with a stern expression, sailed back to her table in the sitting room.
The melancholy silence that followed was broken by the sound of the children's voices and laughter from the next room. Some jolly commotion was plainly going on there.
"Finished, finished!" little Natasha's gleeful shriek rose above the rest.
Pierre exchanged glances with Countess Mary and Nicholas—he never once lost sight of Natasha—and smiled happily.
"That's delightful music!" he said.
"It means Anna Makarovna has finished her stocking," said Countess Mary.

"Oh, I'll go and see," said Pierre, jumping up. "You know," he added, stopping at the door, "why I'm especially fond of that music? It's always the first thing that tells me all is well. When I was driving here today, the closer I got to the house, the more anxious I grew. As soon as I stepped into the anteroom, I heard Andrusha's peals of laughter, and I knew right then that everything was fine."
"I know! I know that feeling," said Nicholas. "But I mustn't go in there—those stockings are supposed to be a surprise for me."
Pierre went off to the children, and the shouting and laughter grew louder still.

"Come, Anna Makarovna," Pierre's voice could be heard saying, "come here, into the middle of the room, and at the word of command, 'One, two'—and when I say 'three'... You stand here, and you in my arms—now then! One, two!..." said Pierre, and a silence fell: "three!"—and a rapturous, breathless shout of children's voices filled the room. "Two, two!" they shouted.

This meant two stockings, which, by some secret method known only to herself, Anna Makarovna would knit at the same time on the same needles, and which, once they were finished, she would always draw out triumphantly, one from inside the other, right in front of the children.
